title: Durham's Water Rules Come Down to the Hose in Your Hand
summary: Sprinklers and pressure washers are banned under Durham's Stage 2 rules. Hand watering is still allowed, and Stage 3 would end it. See what's allowed and how close the trigger is.
body_markdown:
Under the City of Durham's current drought rules, legal yard watering and illegal yard watering can use the same hose. The difference is whether a person is holding it. The city's FAQ defines hand watering as someone physically holding a hose or container fitted with an automatic shutoff. A sprinkler on the end of a hose doesn't count, even if someone is standing next to it.


For homes on City of Durham water, that handheld hose is the main outdoor use of water left. Stage 2 Water Shortage Response took effect June 15, 2026, and the city's[November 2 update](https://durhamnc.gov/CivicAlerts.aspx?AID=4320) confirmed it is still in force. The city's own planning document says the next stage would remove hand watering too. City water staff now describe that next stage as close.


## What still counts as allowed watering


Stage 2 bans spray irrigation of landscapes with City water. The exemptions are short and specific, and most of them involve a person or a slow drip:


- **Hand watering, drip irrigation, and tree or shrub watering bags.**
- **Container plants** , plus commercial plant stock being grown for sale.
- **One day of irrigation after a chemical treatment** that needs immediate watering to protect an existing landscape. That watering can't happen between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m.
- **Short, supervised runs of an irrigation system** to check that it works.
- **Recreational fields, golf courses and botanical sites** that operate under an approved Water Conservation Plan.
- **New-landscape exemptions granted before the shortage was declared** , which are honored until they expire.


The city issues no new exemptions while the shortage declaration is in effect. So a yard planted this fall falls under the same rules as one planted years ago. A new tree with a watering bag, or a shrub bed on drip line, fits within Stage 2. A newly seeded lawn under a rotating sprinkler does not.


The rule hasn't left nurseries out either. In August,[ABC11 reported](https://abc11.com/post/durham-drought-taking-toll-plants-water-restrictions-continue/19714906) that staff at Stone Brothers & Byrd, a Durham garden center, were hand-watering plants three or four times a day. They also turned the water on first thing in the morning, before the sun got high.


## Fall chores that need a different method


Stage 2 reaches well past the lawn. Several jobs that often come up before holiday guests arrive are already off-limits with City water:


1. **Washing the car in the driveway.** Commercial and institutional car washes may keep operating if they meet the ordinance's requirements.
2. **Pressure-washing the house, deck, sidewalk or driveway.** The one exception is cleaning exterior surfaces or decks right before painting or repainting, or when there is a health or safety issue.
3. **Filling decorative fountains and ponds** , unless the water is recycled. Swimming pools may be topped up only to replace water lost to evaporation or spillage and to keep chemical-feed equipment running. These rules carry over from Stage 1 into Stage 2.


Enforcement follows a set sequence in the city FAQ: a warning, then a notice of violation with no fine, then a $100 fine, then a $250 fine, then disconnection of water service. By the time of ABC11's August 21 story, the city had received 320 reports of violations, most of them about sprinkler systems still running. By the November 2 update, the count had reached 475 reports, with 17 violations issued since June 15.


## Why the rules last longer than a good rain


Water is now reaching Durham taps through more routes than usual. The city's November 2 update lists four sources:


1. Lake Michie and Little River Reservoir, Durham's own reservoirs.
2. Part of Durham's Jordan Lake allocation, bought through the Town of Cary.
3. Teer Quarry, which the city is pumping.
4. The Orange Water and Sewer Authority, from which Durham began buying water on November 2.


The Jordan Lake route goes through Cary for a reason.[WRAL reported](https://wral.com/news/local/durham-has-81-days-of-water-remaining-drought-continues-november-2026) that Durham has no infrastructure to draw and treat its Jordan Lake allocation itself. Cary treats the water and sends it through connections between the two systems. In July,[CBS 17 reported](https://cbs17.com/news/local-news/durham-county-news/durham-turns-to-emergency-supply-orange-county-amid-very-serious-water-shortage) that crews had started pumping Teer Quarry, a supply the city hadn't used in almost 20 years.


The city's June notice says Stage 2 stays in place until both reservoirs are full again. According to[Southpoint Access](https://soduwelikelocal.news/durham-water-supply-falls-below-80-days-with-rain-offering-uncertain-relief/) , City figures dated November 5 put combined storage at 31%, down from 33% four days earlier. Readily accessible reservoir water fell from 83 days to 79 over the same stretch. The National Weather Service measured 1.07 inches of rain at Raleigh-Durham International Airport during the storms that came after those figures. Rain at the airport isn't a direct measure of what reached the Lake Michie and Little River watersheds.


The same Southpoint Access report put total estimated supply at 147 days. That figure includes water below the intake structures and Teer Quarry's emergency storage, and the outlet called these planning estimates, not a countdown to dry taps. The NC Drought Management Advisory Council listed Durham County in D2, Severe Drought, as of November 3.


## The step after this one


City water officials sound different now than they did in August. In ABC11's August 21 story, Durham water officials said they did not expect Stage 3 that year. They hoped the rest of hurricane season and winter rain would bring enough water. By early November, the city's update was calling Stage 3 a possibility. Joe Lunne, a senior public information and communications analyst for Durham Water Management, explained the trigger to[WRAL](https://wral.com/news/local/durham-has-81-days-of-water-remaining-drought-continues-november-2026) . The city would move to Stage 3 if forecasts showed at least a 10% chance that combined reservoir storage could drop to 25% within eight weeks.


> "While we are getting close to hitting the trigger for Stage 3, we aren't there yet."


Durham's Water Shortage Response Plan, last updated in December 2016, spells out what Stage 3 would add to the current rules.


Household use Stage 2, in effect now Stage 3, as written in the 2016 plan


Sprinklers and spray irrigation Prohibited Prohibited


Hand watering, drip, tree bags Allowed No irrigation except container plants and commercial plant stock


Washing a car at home Prohibited Prohibited; commercial and institutional car washes may operate


Other outdoor water use Surface washing prohibited, with stated exceptions Prohibited except for emergency fire suppression or public health, safety and welfare


Large users, over 100,000 gallons a day 30% reduction goal 50% reduction goal


The middle row is the change that matters most at home. The handheld hose that keeps a fall-planted tree within the rules today would no longer be an option, though watering plants in containers would still be allowed. The plan also lets the City Manager put a stage in place early or delay lifting one, and stages don't have to go in order.


## Where the current numbers are posted


Durham Water Management posts updates on the[city's Stage 2 page](https://durhamnc.gov/CivicAlerts.aspx?AID=4320) , including storage levels, days of supply and any change in stage. The city also takes violation reports through an online form and through Durham One Call at 919-560-1200. The[city FAQ](https://durhamnc.gov/faq?cat=106) covers definitions such as what counts as hand watering. The rules apply to City-supplied water. Durham serves customers throughout the city and in parts of Durham County, so the provider named on your bill determines which rules apply at your address.


This post is general information, not legal advice. For questions about how the ordinance applies to a specific property, contact Durham Water Management or another qualified professional.
